headline: Wamphassuc Boulders Holding Fluke and Sea Bass — Stripers Have Gone to the Dark
subhead: The rocks off Ram Island and Wamphassuc Point are stacked with bait and bottomfish, but the bass have slipped into a nighttime pattern while the Sound warms from the west.
body_markdown:
The boulders off Wamphassuc Point are wearing a coat of green crab shells this week — small ones, freshly cracked, scattered across the tops of the rocks where the tide drops out at dead low. That's blackfish work, even with the season closed here through the summer. I poled the skiff over that field Tuesday morning on the last of the outgoing and watched three good-sized tog nose up off a boulder the size of a Volkswagen, unbothered, in maybe six feet of water. Nothing to do about it but look — and be glad they're still there for October.

What I can put in the boat right now is fluke and sea bass, and both have been dependable on the current-swept structure through Fishers Island Sound. The water here reads cooler than the rest of the Sound — New London's been sitting around 67.6°F while the western Sound pushes into the low 70s — and that gradient matters. It's kept our rips fishing like rips instead of soup. I've been working the drift between Ram Island and the Fishers Island shore, 18 to 25 feet, dragging a 3/4-ounce white bucktail tipped with a strip of squid or a 4-inch chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet. Fluke to 4 pounds have come off that stretch on the last two hours of the ebb, when the current pulls hard enough to hold the boat on a controlled drift but not so hard you're bouncing bottom every other cast. Keeper counts have been honest — not a banner week, but two or three fish to the boat most trips, mixed with plenty of shorts that keep you paying attention.

Sea bass have been the better story. Hard bottom off Watch Hill Reef and the eastern end of Fishers Island Sound is holding a strong resident population — I heard of a 28-inch fish taken out that way recently, which tells you the population's got some age and size to it this year. I've been anchoring up on the structure with a high-low rig, squid strips and a chunk of clam, dropping straight down in 25 to 35 feet on the slower stages of the tide. Slack water and the first hour of a new tide have been the windows — once the current gets running hard, the sea bass tuck in tight to the rocks and won't leave.

Stripers are the tricky part of this report, and I want to be straight about it. The warm push from the western Sound has shoved bass into a nocturnal pattern almost everywhere south and west of us — daytime bites have gone quiet as the fish avoid the heat and feed after dark. Our water's a few degrees cooler thanks to that thermal gradient off New London, so we're getting a little more daytime activity than the boats working closer to the city, but it's still best at the edges of light — first hour after sunrise, last hour before dark, and through the night on the boulder fields off Esker Point and the mouth of the Mystic River. I've been running unweighted eels and 2-ounce bucktails over structure on the last two hours of the incoming, letting the current sweep the offering across the rock piles rather than working it hard. Fish have been there but not stacked — a few good bass in the 28- to 34-inch range each trip I've put in after dark, nothing you'd call consistent, but enough to make the late nights worth it if you're patient with the presentation.

One thing worth watching closely over the next week or two: we flagged the bonito setup last week, and the water's lining up the way we thought it would. Block Island's holding water in the high 60s now, well within the range bonito want, and that kind of temperature typically means a push into eastern Long Island Sound within a week or ten days. Nothing's shown yet off Watch Hill Reef or Napatree Point, but I'd keep a light spinning rod rigged with a small metal — a Deadly Dick or a 1-ounce Kastmaster — on the console starting now. When that first scout shows on the surface working bait against the current, you want to be ready, because the window before everybody else notices is short.

Tide's easing toward the first quarter moon on the 21st, which should soften the current through the rips over the next several days. That's actually good news for the fluke and sea bass game — slower water lets you work a bucktail more deliberately instead of fighting the drift, and both species have been responding better to a controlled presentation than a fast one. For the stripers, I'd lean into the dark hours through this stretch and target the boulder fields where current breaks hard against structure — Ram Island's north side, the rocks off Esker Point, and the drop just outside the Stonington Breakwater. If the bonito scouts do show early, my money's on Napatree first, given the exposure to open water and the bait that's been stacking there. Until then, it's a rocks-and-patience week — nothing spectacular, but honest fishing if you put in the time on the right stage of tide.
